name: Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma
lead: Which gate this patient is at, and what the next act must not foreclose — drainage before extent, extent before tissue, and the transplant question before palliative therapy.
gatelabel: The decision in front of you

gates.name: 0 · Biliary drainage comes first
crit: Cholangitis, or a bilirubin that is rising
Jaundice in a patient whose planned operation is a major hepatectomy with a predicted future liver remnant of 30% or less
Portal vein embolisation planned — hypertrophy is poor while the remnant stays cholestatic
Neoadjuvant chemoradiation, radiotherapy or systemic therapy planned
Malnutrition, or hepatic or renal insufficiency from prolonged jaundice
Note that routine preoperative drainage of every jaundiced patient is not what the guidelines say: this is an indication list, not a default
gates.ask: Which sectors am I draining, and does an operative plan exist yet to tell me which ones they are?

standard.t: Drain the sectors that will form the future liver remnant, not the most accessible duct, and name one owner for the drainage strategy.
standard.pref: Every patient drained with a resection or protocol destination in mind — the objective is decompression of the sectors you intend to keep, which is why Gate 0 and the resectability gate are discussed together at the first tumour board. ESGE 2026 suggests against routine preoperative drainage and lists severe jaundice, cholangitis and a predicted remnant of 30% or less as the accepted indications (conditional, low quality); the Milan consensus restricts it to a small remnant needing hypertrophy, cholangitis, renal or hepatic failure, severe malnutrition or pruritus, and says to drain the future liver remnant exclusively.
standard.avoid: Do not drain an atrophic or to-be-resected lobe: it relieves jaundice without enabling the operation, and hypertrophy after portal vein embolisation is poor in a liver that remains cholestatic. Cholangitis after a poorly planned drain is the most common avoidable disaster in this disease. Equally, do not drain reflexively: the Coelen investigators' own conclusion from their trial was that drainage should follow resectability assessment at a specialist centre and may be unnecessary when the remnant exceeds 50% of liver volume.
standard.note: Grade D. No trial compares remnant-focused drainage with draining the most accessible duct; the position follows from the physiology of hypertrophy in a cholestatic liver and from the guidelines' own wording, not from comparative outcome data. The Asia-Pacific panel reached only 56% full agreement on its preoperative-drainage statement. Antibiotics with the procedure, cultures sent, and a named owner for drain management. As few drains as achieve remnant decompression — multiple uncoordinated drains placed by different services is a recognised failure pattern. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: In unresectable disease being drained for palliation, aim to drain more than 50% of viable liver volume including the future liver remnant, and drain every segment that has been opacified.
standard.pref: Palliative drainage where the destination is systemic therapy or symptom control. ESGE 2026 raises the target to 70% or more where it can be achieved; above 50% drained gave better clinical success (OR 4.5) and longer survival (119 versus 59 days), and the Asia-Pacific statement reports longer survival above 80% drained (HR 2.46).
standard.avoid: Generally do not drain atrophic segments, and do not inject contrast into a duct you do not intend to drain — an opacified undrained sector is a cholangitis waiting to happen.
standard.note: Downgraded to D: no threshold here was derived. ESGE lists prospective volumetry against survival and access to chemotherapy as an unmet need, and no meta-analysis or comparative trial has tested any percentage cut-off; the supporting cohorts disagree among themselves (50%, 71%, 80%) and the 50% and 80% figures come from single-centre retrospective series (Vienne 2010, Caillol 2019) with no prospective validation. Both the ESGE and Asia-Pacific statements on this are graded low or very low quality. Sector volumes for planning: right anterior, right posterior and left each about 30%, segments I and IV about 10%, atrophic segments counted as non-viable. Bismuth I, II and IIIb can often be served by one stent; IIIa and IV need two or more to reach 50%.

opts.name: Endoscopic drainage (ERCP)
opts.when: ESGE 2026 recommends ERCP over percutaneous drainage for preoperative drainage in malignant hilar obstruction (strong recommendation, moderate quality), and ASGE suggests against routine percutaneous drainage as first-line therapy before possible resection or transplantation (conditional, low quality). NCCN leaves route to local expertise after multidisciplinary review.
opts.pref: The first route in a patient who still has a curative option, where the anatomy is reachable and the endoscopic service is experienced. DRAINAGE was stopped early because mortality between randomisation and 90 days after surgery was higher after percutaneous drainage, 11 of 27 (41%) versus 3 of 27 (11%), relative risk 3.67 (95% CI 1.15–11.69), p=0.03; a 1,085-patient meta-analysis found more implantation metastases after the percutaneous route (OR 0.35, 0.23–0.53).
opts.avoid: Lower technical success (20 of 27, 74%, versus 25 of 27, 93%) and more pancreatitis (5, 19%, versus 1, 4%). In the trial 15 of 27 patients allocated to endoscopic drainage (56%) needed additional percutaneous drainage against 1 of 27 the other way, so this is a comparison of initial strategies, not of techniques. ESGE's own section cites a meta-analysis giving percutaneous drainage higher therapeutic success (OR 3.5, 95% CI 2.1–6.0) and 11.5-fold more reintervention after ERCP, with 10 of its 11 studies retrospective — the strong recommendation runs against the best comparative data printed beside it.

opts.name: Percutaneous transhepatic drainage
opts.when: Reserved for failed or anatomically unsuitable endoscopic access, and accepted either way for palliative drainage of unresectable disease, by patient preference, disease characteristics and local expertise.
opts.pref: Sectors that endoscopic drainage cannot reach, particularly in Bismuth IIIa and IV disease, and where percutaneous delineation of intrahepatic tumour spread will change the operative plan. It is also the route with the higher technical success in the one randomised comparison and in ESGE's pooled data.
opts.avoid: Weigh the catheter-tract and peritoneal seeding concern heavily in anyone who may be a transplant protocol candidate: ASGE's recommendation rests on 7.8% seeding after endoscopic versus 17.1% after percutaneous drainage (OR 0.27, 0.13–0.56), with percutaneous drainage the only independent predictor of peritoneal recurrence in one adjusted cohort (OR 6.9, 1.9–25.7). Read that at its real strength — the ASGE panel itself calls this the weakest evidence in the document: a six-study meta-analysis with high heterogeneity (I² 66%) and very few events, plus one adjusted single-centre cohort, both graded very low quality.

standard.order: Downgraded from B to C. The order reflects guideline wording and one prematurely stopped trial, not a demonstrated survival advantage. The roadmap's own position is that route is unsettled: DRAINAGE was negative on its primary endpoint — one or more severe drainage-related complications in 17 of 27 (63%) after percutaneous versus 18 of 27 (67%) after endoscopic drainage, relative risk 0.94 (95% CI 0.64–1.40) — and the mortality signal that stopped it came from 54 of a planned 106 patients, is acknowledged by the authors as prone to type I error, and had no mechanism identified by the safety board. Pooled across three randomised trials, ASGE found 30-day mortality only trending lower with endoscopic drainage (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.28–1.01, p=0.05). What is not optional is draining the correct sectors.
standard.flagnote: Ratification item (§11 item 2): should the roadmap name endoscopic drainage as the default first route for potential resection and protocol candidates, as AASLD and ESGE 2026 do, or keep route unsettled as written? The 2015 AHPBA consensus preferred the percutaneous route and that preference has not held up, but the 2026 reversal rests on a single stopped trial extrapolated from the preoperative to the palliative setting. Note before ratifying: five ESGE authors declare relationships with stent manufacturers, many ASGE panel members declare the same, and one ASGE panel member is at this institution. Registry: route, cholangitis, re-intervention.

alt.t: A removable plastic stent while resection, transplantation or a good systemic response remains possible; an uncovered metal stent once those options are closed.
alt.pref: Patients whose drainage strategy is not yet defined, or who may respond well to systemic therapy and outlive uncovered-stent patency.
alt.avoid: Avoid uncovered metal stents in a potential transplant candidate — they cannot be removed and are difficult to deal with surgically. Metal stents give better patency and fewer reinterventions (OR 0.34) and 56 days more survival (95% CI 12–101) in the pooled ASGE analysis, but the comparator plastic arms were waited out to occlusion rather than exchanged on schedule, which is why the ASGE panel declined a strong recommendation.
alt.note: The roadmap itself does not set a stent rule — it says to choose stent and access route through multidisciplinary review, and that the algorithm does not establish a universal stent material. The rule above is the alignment worksheet's proposal (area 3) and needs ratification. The page also takes no position on bilateral versus unilateral stenting, which is a live question: ASGE suggests bilateral absent lobar atrophy, but its pooled survival gain was 11 days (95% CI −12 to 35) and pooled patency showed no difference (SMD 0.38, −0.22 to 0.99, I² 78%), while one randomised trial reported in ESGE 2026 gave bilateral stenting clinical success 95.3% versus 84.9% and patency 252 versus 139 days.

avoid.t: Do not place the first stent before multiphase CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis and MRI with MRCP, unless cholangitis or a rapidly rising bilirubin makes drainage urgent.
avoid.pref: Document the reason when emergency decompression comes first, and complete staging promptly.
avoid.avoid: A stent's inflammatory change degrades assessment of ductal extent and cannot be undone. MRI/MRCP outperforms contrast-enhanced CT both for the nature of the stricture (pooled accuracy 96% versus 89%, OR 2.1, 1.2–3.6) and for identifying the level (OR 3.3, 1.2–9.1).
avoid.note: Downgraded from B to C: the ESGE recommendation behind these numbers is conditional on low-quality evidence, and the ESGE panel found no randomised trial for any of its perihilar questions.

avoid.t: Do not accept a bilirubin threshold that has not been written down.
avoid.pref: Set the programme threshold locally, record it, and apply it consistently before major hepatectomy, embolic therapy, radiation and systemic therapy.
avoid.avoid: There are no comparative data defining the cut-off; it is a safety convention, and an unwritten one is applied inconsistently. §11 item 3 audits post-hepatectomy liver failure by preoperative bilirubin.

gates.name: 1 · Define the extent
crit: Multiphase CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus MRI with MRCP, obtained before stenting where the clinical situation allows
Biliary extent recorded by sector, with portal venous and hepatic arterial involvement and lobar atrophy
Future liver remnant volume, regional and distant nodal status, peritoneal findings
Bilirubin trajectory and performance status
Whether the patient has primary sclerosing cholangitis — it changes both the differential and the transplant discussion
gates.ask: Do I know the extent well enough to say whether this is resectable, and did I get the imaging before anyone stented?

standard.t: Stage with multiphase CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis plus MRI with MRCP; chest imaging is part of staging because distant spread changes every later gate.
standard.pref: Every patient, before elective instrumentation. CT and MRI are complementary and both are required; MRCP comes before ERC to avoid artefact. The AHPBA panel states a well-performed CT or MRI should exceed 75% accuracy for resectability.
standard.avoid: FDG-PET lacks the sensitivity and specificity for routine staging in this disease and should not replace the cross-sectional package — though note BSG 2023 does recommend FDG-PET/CT for nodal and distant disease, so this is a point of guideline disagreement, not settled fact.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C. The 75% accuracy figure is an ungraded expert-consensus statement from a six-person panel across four institutions, and the ESGE imaging recommendation that supports MRI/MRCP over CT is conditional on low-quality evidence. Nothing here was derived prospectively in perihilar disease.

standard.t: Record the Bismuth-Corlette type as shorthand for the pattern of ductal involvement, but do not let it decide resectability — vascular involvement, lobar atrophy, nodal status and remnant volume do that.
standard.pref: Communication at the board, and planning which sectors to drain and how many stents it will take.
standard.avoid: Do not treat the preoperative type as the final extent. In the original series postoperative histology upstaged tumours, 4 operative type IV lesions becoming 9, so the preoperative type systematically understates extent. The Milan jury declined to endorse Bismuth-Corlette, or any other staging system — MSKCC included — as a predictor of resectability, and its own resectability criteria are stated to be expert opinion requiring validation.
standard.note: Grade C, and read the denominators: the classification and its type-specific operations rest on 23 resections accumulated over 30 years at one centre, one to four patients per type, in 122 patients taken to surgery. See the quick reference for the operation each type implies.

standard.t: Treat CA 19-9 and CEA as supporting measurements, not proof of malignancy, and record each value with the bilirubin and drainage status at the time it was drawn.
standard.pref: Where a value is to count toward the transplant protocol's diagnostic criteria it is measured only after decompression and in the absence of cholangitis.
standard.avoid: Tumour markers must not be used alone to separate a benign from a malignant stricture: pooled accuracy is 81% (76–87) for CA 19-9 and 70% (62–78) for CEA, with false-positive rates of 15% and 18%, and CA 19-9 rises in primary sclerosing cholangitis, cirrhosis and obstructive jaundice. NCCN is explicit that CEA and CA 19-9 are baseline tests and should not be done to confirm the diagnosis.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C: the ESGE recommendation is conditional on very low quality evidence. This matters more here than elsewhere, because CA 19-9 above 100 U/mL is one of the alternative diagnostic criteria for the transplant protocol — a 15% false-positive rate sits underneath a listing decision.

alt.t: Measure the future liver remnant by CT volumetry and state the threshold the board is working to before committing to augmentation.
alt.pref: Any patient in whom an extended hepatectomy is contemplated. AASLD recommends an adequate remnant of at least 30%; BSG uses 20% with normal parenchyma, 30% after chemotherapy and 40% with cirrhosis; the Milan consensus uses 30% if healthy and at least 40% if frail, cholangitic, cholestatic or malnourished, standardised by Vauthey's formula.
alt.avoid: A cholestatic liver fits none of those categories cleanly, which is the roadmap's reason for leaving the number to the board rather than copying one.
alt.note: Downgraded from C to D. None of these thresholds was derived: three guidelines give three different numbers for the same decision, the Milan figure sits at level-4 expert opinion, and no comparative study tests one cut-off against another in perihilar disease. The roadmap states no numeric remnant threshold. Whether to adopt AASLD's single 30% or BSG's parenchyma-adjusted 20/30/40% is §11 item 4 territory and needs specialty approval.

avoid.t: Do not carry an iCCA or distal cholangiocarcinoma pathway into this disease.
avoid.pref: Perihilar disease has its own gates: central biliary and vascular anatomy and longitudinal tumour spread differ from a small peripheral liver mass, and the transplant route, the biopsy constraint and the drainage problem are all specific to it.
avoid.avoid: Intrahepatic and distal cholangiocarcinoma are covered separately and are not interchangeable with this pathway. Gallbladder cancer is out of scope.

gates.name: 2 · Tissue — what the destination needs, and what the route costs
crit: The destination is named before any needle is passed: resection, transplant protocol, or systemic therapy
Transperitoneal routes — percutaneous, operative and endoscopic ultrasound — are off the table in anyone who may be protocol-eligible
Tissue is taken at the index ERCP, before or at the time the first stent is placed
A separate specimen from the same ERCP goes for molecular testing where it is available
Nodal sampling and sampling of the primary are treated as different decisions
gates.ask: Do I actually need tissue for where this patient is going, and will the route I am about to use cost them an option?

standard.t: A transperitoneal biopsy of the primary tumour must be avoided in any patient who may be protocol-eligible — and that includes the endoscopic ultrasound route.
standard.pref: Discuss the route with the transplant team before obtaining tissue. OPTN Policy 9.5.A, requirement 6 names percutaneous, operative and endoscopic ultrasound routes: an EUS needle reaching a perihilar tumour crosses the peritoneal cavity, so it counts. Avoidance is a condition of the standardized exception, not a weighing of evidence — taking the route removes the patient from the standardized route entirely.
standard.avoid: In the Mayo protocol cohort of 191 patients, 16 had a transperitoneal fine-needle aspiration of the primary elsewhere; of the 6 whose aspirate was positive for adenocarcinoma, 5 of 6 (83%) had peritoneal metastases at operative staging, against 8% (14 of 175) in those not biopsied (P=0.0097). The 9 patients with non-diagnostic aspirates had no metastases at all. The two groups did not differ in age, sex, PSC, presence or size of a mass, presenting CA 19-9 or interval to staging.
standard.note: The grade records an absolute policy condition, not the strength of the evidence underneath it, and the two must not be confused. The evidence is six exposed patients and five events: that cannot support a risk estimate, it is not a measured seeding rate, and the roadmap does not present it as one. Because only diagnostic aspirates carried the excess, a positive aspirate may partly be marking a tumour bulky and cell-rich enough to hit with a needle rather than causing dissemination; reverse causation is not excluded by this retrospective single-programme design, and no histological features were available to match the groups on. Only patients already accepted onto the protocol were counted, so anyone whose outside aspirate took them out of consideration is invisible. The 12-centre series is often quoted here too, but its hazard ratio of 2.98 (95% CI 1.79–4.95) is for a composite off-criteria group — 21 patients with a mass over 3 cm, 16 with a direct tumour biopsy, 4 with metastases and 7 with a prior malignancy — and is not attributable to biopsy alone.

standard.t: Take tissue at the index ERCP, with brush cytology completed by fluoroscopy-guided intraductal biopsies wherever that is technically feasible.
standard.pref: Every patient having a first ERCP for a malignant-appearing hilar stricture. ASGE pools 21 studies and 2,726 patients: incremental yield of adding biopsy to brushing 20% (95% CI 9–31), sensitivity 0.66 combined against 0.52 for biopsy and 0.40 for brushing alone (P<.001). ESGE's figure is higher but rests on far less — a pooled incremental yield of 25% (11–38, OR 2.7, 1.5–4.9) from two retrospective cohorts totalling 101 patients. The Asia-Pacific statement quotes combined sensitivity about 70% against 21–56% for brushing alone and 43–67% for intraductal biopsy.
standard.avoid: Deferring tissue to a later stent exchange is treated as costless in practice and probably is not. Note also that adding biopsy is not free: in the ASGE analysis there was no overall difference in adverse events (OR 0.53, 0.14–2.05) but the biopsy arm carried two severe events, prolonged bleeding and a perforation needing surgical choledochotomy.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C: every recommendation in both guidelines on this question is conditional on low or very low quality evidence, and neither panel found a randomised trial for any perihilar question. How much tissue is itself unsettled — ESGE says three to four intraductal biopsies appear sufficient, while the real-world cholangioscopy cohort below took a median of 3 and had 33% inconclusive specimens, and its authors recommend a minimum of four. Cytology sensitivity rises with brush passes: 38% at 10, 47% at 20 and 57% at 30 in a multicentre randomised trial of more than 400 patients. For an indeterminate stricture, add cholangioscopy-guided biopsies — pooled incremental yield 27% (10–45) from 13 studies and 1,529 patients, sensitivity 0.72 against 0.61 — but do not repeat the guidelines' claim that this costs nothing: the PSC meta-analysis records post-procedure cholangitis in 11% and procedural failure in 15% of PSC ducts against 2% of controls, and the Groningen cohort had adverse events in 10 of 80 (13%), including two episodes of cholangitis and one cardiac arrest with subsequent stroke.

standard.t: Send a separate specimen from the same ERCP for next-generation sequencing: it raises yield on the one route that does not jeopardise protocol candidacy.
standard.pref: Potential protocol candidates above all, where confirmed malignancy is a protocol condition and the route that would most readily provide it is the one route excluded. In a 6-year prospective study of 2,908 ERCP-obtained specimens from 2,116 patients at 28 US institutions, with accuracy computed on the 1,979 patients who had follow-up (1,108 neoplastic, 871 benign), a DNA/RNA panel gave 82% sensitivity and 98% specificity for a neoplastic stricture, against 44% and 99% for pathological assessment of separate specimens; combining the two gave 88% at 97%. In intrahepatic or hilar strictures specifically it was 80% versus 36%, and 86% combined. Actionable alterations were found in 23% of positive malignancies and in 137 of 458 cholangiocarcinomas (30%), so the same specimen can serve diagnosis and target identification. Assay failure was about 1%. [PAYER] [DEVICE]
standard.avoid: Four cautions. Specificity is high but not perfect, and a false positive commits a patient to neoadjuvant chemoradiation and transplantation — the consequence of error is not symmetrical with the consequence in an ordinary diagnostic setting; sixteen false positives occurred, at variant allele frequencies of 1.5–30%. The endpoint was a neoplastic stricture, which is broader than malignancy, and a stricture could be called neoplastic on imaging plus clinical or radiographic progression over 12 months rather than on tissue, which tends to flatter the test that often prompted that work-up. Only 2% of neoplastic strictures were purely dysplastic, so outside PSC this is earlier diagnosis of established cancer, not early detection, and no survival or resectability benefit has been shown. And a negative result still does not exclude malignancy.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C. Identical specimens were never compared — sequencing and pathology were run on different specimens — specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, FISH was never compared head to head, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. The earlier single-centre prospective study (252 patients, 346 specimens) raised pathology sensitivity from 35% to 71% on 132 paired brushings and from 52% to 75% on 114 paired biopsies, and reported 83% versus 8% in primary sclerosing cholangitis on 12 malignant cases (95% CI 0.51–0.98). Two real-world cohorts reproduce the overall direction (65% versus 52% alone and 78% combined on 47 biopsies in one; 75% versus 42.9% in 77 patients in the other) but neither supports the PSC result — one found 20% sensitivity in PSC against 40% for brush cytology — and in the one cohort that reported it separately, the gain in cholangiocarcinoma itself was not significant (70% versus 60%, P=.72). The test is a laboratory-developed test from a single CLIA-certified laboratory, not FDA cleared, and coverage must be verified in writing before it is written into routine practice.

opts.name: Proceed to resection without tissue
opts.when: NCCN: surgery may be performed when the index of suspicion is high, and biopsy is not required. BSG accepts surgery without histological certainty. The AHPBA consensus states pathologic confirmation is not required before resection or before starting the transplant protocol.
opts.pref: A malignant-appearing stricture with no alternative explanation, where the operative plan would not change whatever the result. The biopsy route is unconstrained in a resection-only candidate — biopsy does not foreclose resection.
opts.avoid: A benign aetiology is found in about 10% of resections done on a presumptive diagnosis by the AHPBA panel's figure, and about 15% in a 30-year tertiary series, in an operation whose 90-day mortality reaches 13% even in benchmark patients at expert centres. Do not use it to skip the transplant question in a patient who might be a protocol candidate.

opts.name: EUS-guided aspiration of the primary
opts.when: ESGE suggests EUS-guided tissue acquisition for perihilar strictures only when ERCP-based modalities are insufficient and 'provided that curative resection is not feasible and/or when cross-sectional imaging has shown accessible extraluminal disease' (conditional, low quality). Pooled EUS sensitivity 78% (70–86), accuracy 84% (78–91), incremental yield over ERCP 33%.
opts.pref: Established unresectable disease with no transplant option, where a tissue diagnosis is needed to start systemic therapy and ERCP sampling has failed. Where the stricture proves distal rather than perihilar, EUS-guided acquisition becomes the higher-yield route and carries no protocol penalty.
opts.avoid: Never in a potential protocol candidate. ESGE itself notes that the hilar seeding risk is supported in this disease by one retrospective series of 150 patients, with the rest extrapolated from pancreatic adenocarcinoma and percutaneous aspiration, and makes no recommendation for transplant candidates — so for protocol candidates the constraint rests on OPTN Policy 9.5.A and the Mayo data, not on ESGE. ASGE is explicit that if EUS is performed for a proximal or hilar stricture the endosonographer should not sample the biliary mass itself.

opts.name: EUS evaluation and aspiration of regional nodes
opts.when: AASLD requires EUS-FNA of regional nodes before neoadjuvant therapy in patients being evaluated for transplantation; BSG samples an involved locoregional node for staging while leaving the mass alone.
opts.pref: Before a transplant workup is spent. Node-positive disease is itself a protocol exclusion, so a positive nodal result does not cost candidacy that existed — it identifies a patient who was never a candidate.
opts.avoid: Do not let a nodal pass become a pass at the primary; they are different sampling targets. AASLD also notes that no morphological criteria reliably identify malignant nodes, which weakens a 'suspicious node' trigger, and the AASLD document is explicitly expert consensus rather than a GRADE-rated guideline.

alt.order: Ordered by what the destination requires, not by diagnostic yield. The pooled comparison that favours EUS over ERCP — mean sensitivity 75% versus 49%, specificity 100% versus 96% — comes from 294 patients at a pretest probability of 77%, is not specific to perihilar disease, and only 3 of its 8 studies applied both tests to the same patients; three of its proximal-stricture studies enrolled patients only after ERCP sampling had already failed, which guarantees a low ERCP figure by design. QUADAS-2 scored all eight studies at high risk of selection bias, the results are simple means rather than a pooled bivariate model, and the review never mentions that transperitoneal aspiration disqualifies a transplant candidate. Negative predictive values were 47% (SD 14.73) and 34% (SD 24.63), so on either modality a negative result excludes nothing — and those standard deviations are as large as the estimates.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item (§11 item 6): how tissue is obtained in a potentially protocol-eligible patient needs a standing agreement, so that no one disqualifies a candidate inadvertently. §11 item 8: whether a molecular result satisfies the protocol's confirmed-malignancy condition is a governance decision the published criteria do not address — agree it with the transplant team in advance, not case by case. Audit: biopsy route in protocol candidates; NGS result, protocol decision, explant finding.

alt.t: Where a stent is already in place, take tissue after removing it and send material for molecular testing — and do not assume cholangioscopic biopsy will outperform the brush.
alt.pref: The referred patient who arrives already stented — a common presentation, and the one where the published yields cannot be assumed to apply.
alt.avoid: Do not treat a negative result as reassuring, and do not treat cholangioscopy as the answer here. In the real-world Groningen cohort of 80 patients, 70 (88%) had had a previous ERCP, 44 (55%) had a plastic stent removed at the start of the procedure and 32 (40%) had primary sclerosing cholangitis: cholangioscopy-guided biopsy sensitivity was 15% (95% CI 0–31), far below the 65% (35–87) pooled from 4 studies and 128 PSC patients that did not report stent status, and visual assessment was 64% sensitive with 62% specificity. Brush cytology taken at the same procedure beat both — sensitivity 47%, specificity 95%, accuracy 81%, diagnostic odds ratio 19.6 against 6.6 for the targeted biopsy. Management changed in only 13 of 77 (17%).
alt.note: Downgraded to D, and the roadmap's earlier wording is withdrawn: the one cohort that tested a blind brush against cholangioscopy after stent removal found the brush better, so recommending cholangioscopic sampling instead of a brush is not supported. The low biopsy figure is also as much about technique as about the stent — a median of 3 biopsies with 33% of specimens inconclusive, 66 of 80 procedures on a first-generation device, and authors who recommend a minimum of four biopsies. No study quantifies sampling yield stratified by prior stent placement; targeted searches for it return nothing, and this pathway should not imply otherwise. Mechanistically stents do produce reactive change: in a blinded multi-reviewer study of 60 brushings — 30 malignant and 30 benign, half the benign cases previously stented — necrosis (17% versus 13%) and infiltrating inflammation (43% versus 33%) did not distinguish malignancy, 3 or more of 11 cytological characteristics gave sensitivity 70% at specificity 97%, and 7 of 30 malignant brushings showed none of them. That study was enriched 50:50 by design, so its predictive values do not transfer to clinic.

avoid.t: Do not pass a needle across the peritoneum toward a perihilar tumour in a patient who still has a curative option.
avoid.pref: Keep a mandatory local pre-biopsy transplant gate: before biopsy, evaluate whether the patient is a resection or transplant candidate.
avoid.avoid: Also avoid an exploratory resection attempt that violates the tumour plane in a borderline candidate — AASLD and the programme's own protocol list surgical violation of the tumour plane as a transplant exclusion, and the roadmap's route logic covers needles only.
avoid.note: The roadmap is internally inconsistent here and says so: its §4 Resection row calls the biopsy route unconstrained, while this callout extends the rule to anyone with a curative option, which includes resection. BSG states the stricter rule, and a resection candidate judged unresectable before any operative violation of the tumour plane may become a protocol candidate. Unresolved — see the honest section.

avoid.t: Do not keep resampling in pursuit of a negative result that will not be believed.
avoid.pref: Decide in advance what a negative result will change. If the answer is nothing, the patient needs a destination decision, not another ERCP.
avoid.avoid: Negative predictive values are 34% for ERCP-based sampling and 47% for EUS aspiration in a 294-patient meta-analysis at 77% pretest probability, so with either modality a negative result does not exclude malignancy; repeated sampling is a common way to lose time. FISH trisomy or tetrasomy alone is uninformative (sensitivity 31%, 22–40; specificity 71%, 67–75; positive likelihood ratio 1.19, 0.65–2.21). Only polysomy carries information (51%, 43–59, and 93%, 91–95), and it is a named protocol criterion — but its positive predictive value in PSC was only 0.68 (0.58–0.76), and all eight studies in that meta-analysis came from a single centre with overlapping recruitment windows.
avoid.note: Downgraded from B to C. Both pooled estimates rest on analyses the spec's own standard would not call B: the ERCP-versus-EUS review scored high risk of selection bias in every included study and reported simple means, and the FISH meta-analysis is effectively one institution's experience with likely verification bias, since a FISH-positive patient is more likely to reach the surgery that classifies them.

gates.name: 3 · Resectable disease
crit: Biliary and vascular extent that permits a technically achievable R0 resection
Contralateral liver with intact arterial and portal inflow as well as biliary drainage
Future liver remnant adequate, or made adequate by embolisation after the remnant has been drained
No intrahepatic, extrahepatic, nodal or peritoneal metastases on the staging package
Patient fit for extended hepatectomy with biliary reconstruction, at a centre that does them
gates.ask: Can I take this out with a negative margin and leave behind a liver that works?

standard.t: Extended hepatectomy with en bloc extrahepatic bile duct resection, regional lymphadenectomy and biliary reconstruction, with portal vein resection and reconstruction where it is required to achieve R0.
standard.pref: Technically resectable disease in a fit patient. Margin status drives everything: in the original series survival with clear margins (n=9) was 100%, 71% and 50% at 1, 2 and 3 years, against 82%, 43% and 12% with microscopic residual disease (n=10) and death within 32 months in all four patients with gross residual disease. Local recurrence followed a positive microscopic margin in every case but one, and occurred in no patient whose margin was histologically free. Across series, R0 gives median survival 27–58 months and 5-year survival 27–45%, against 12–21 months and 0–23% with a positive margin.
standard.avoid: Do not attempt local excision alone above Bismuth type I: all five type II and IIIa patients treated that way had involved margins and recurred locally. Caudate resection is obligatory from type II upward because the segment 1 ducts are almost always involved. The Milan consensus prefers left-sided hemihepatectomy where it will achieve the same clearance, because right-sided resection carries more morbidity, liver failure and mortality at equal oncological outcome, and does not recommend routine vascular resection, no-touch technique included; arterial resection belongs in expert centres only.
standard.note: Downgraded from B to C. The margin data come from 23 resections accumulated over 30 years at one centre — 19 of 122 operated patients (15.6%) had a macroscopically curative resection and only 9 of 122 (7.4%) a histologically negative margin — with no comparison group, mean follow-up 26 months, and the survival credited to R0 therefore uncontrolled and heavily selected. The 27–58 month R0 figure is ungraded expert consensus. Outcomes are volume-dependent: even in benchmark patients at expert centres 5-year overall survival does not exceed 40%, severe complications reach 70%, 90-day mortality reaches 13%, one in five needs re-laparotomy and only two-thirds achieve a negative margin. Lymphadenectomy of stations 12 (positive in 25%), 8 (14%) and 13a (11%) with 5–7 nodes harvested; nodal positivity runs 16–60% overall; no benefit from extended dissection to the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery or periaortic nodes. [EXPERTISE]

standard.t: Prepare in a sequence with dates rather than improvising: drain the remnant, embolise the portal vein when the remnant is inadequate, correct nutrition.
standard.pref: Every patient needing an extended hepatectomy. These steps take weeks, and the order is not interchangeable — hypertrophy is poor while the remnant remains obstructed, so drainage comes first.

opts.name: Portal vein embolisation
opts.when: Recommended where the anticipated remnant is inadequate and the disease is otherwise resectable. NCCN requires the contralateral liver to have intact arterial and portal inflow as well as biliary drainage.
opts.pref: Most useful when the future liver remnant is below 30–40%. A meta-analysis of 1,140 patients found remnant gains of 8–27% with no mortality and under 3% morbidity.
opts.avoid: Do not embolise a remnant that is still obstructed. If the post-embolisation remnant is 20% or less, or hypertrophy is 5% or less, resection may be contraindicated — reassess at 3–6 weeks and check remnant drainage and nutrition before abandoning the operation.

opts.name: Liver venous deprivation
opts.when: The Milan consensus places it after portal vein embolisation, for a remnant under 20–25% — a level-4 expert-opinion statement with no comparative data in this disease.
opts.pref: Expert centres where portal vein embolisation alone will not deliver the volume needed.
opts.avoid: Not a first manoeuvre, and not a substitute for drainage of the remnant.

opts.name: ALPPS
opts.when: Salvage only in the Milan consensus; BSG does not recommend it for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma at all.
opts.pref: No routine place in this disease.
opts.avoid: Mortality was 48% in the international registry for perihilar cholangiocarcinoma.

alt.order: Ordered as the guidelines order augmentation, not by comparative survival data — no trial compares these in perihilar disease, and the Milan recommendations on augmentation sit at level 4. The registry mortality figure for ALPPS is the one hard number in the group and it argues against it.
alt.flagnote: Ratification item (§11 item 4, and alignment area 11): the roadmap states no numeric remnant threshold and does not list ALPPS in its Avoid row. The alignment worksheet recommends adding both — a written threshold makes the embolisation decision auditable, and BSG's 48% registry mortality is strong enough to justify an explicit Avoid line. Audit: volume, 90-day mortality, R0 rate.

alt.t: Capecitabine for 6 months is a reasonable option after resection, not an obligation — offer it with the actual numbers.
alt.pref: A resected patient fit for 8 cycles who wants adjuvant treatment, particularly with adverse features. BILCAP (n=447) gave median overall survival 51.1 versus 36.4 months with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097 — the intention-to-treat primary analysis did not meet significance. Significance appeared per protocol (210 versus 220 patients, HR 0.75, 0.58–0.97) and in the protocol-specified intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis adjusted for nodal status, grade and sex (HR 0.71, 0.55–0.92), and the trial was unmasked.
alt.avoid: Do not present it as established benefit in this tumour. 128 of 447 patients (29%) had hilar tumours, the trial was not powered for site-specific effects, and the Milan consensus records that these trials showed no benefit in the perihilar subgroup. The recurrence-free survival advantage was confined to the first 24 months (HR 0.75, 0.58–0.98) with none from 24 to 60 months (HR 1.48, 0.80–2.77), which the authors read as recurrence deferred rather than prevented. Grade 3 events occurred in 44% of treated patients, 55% completed all eight cycles, 46% needed a dose reduction and 32% stopped for toxicity.
alt.note: Downgraded from B to C, because the trial is negative on its prespecified primary endpoint and the positive signal rests on a per-protocol analysis and an adjusted model; the linked commentary asks whether that is enough to define a standard of care. NCCN designates capecitabine preferred, category 1, while also acknowledging BILCAP's nonsignificant intention-to-treat analysis; the local label and grade remain more cautious and require explicit multidisciplinary ratification. ASCOT (n=440) was positive for S-1 — 3-year survival 77.1% versus 67.6%, HR 0.69 (0.51–0.94) — but relapse-free survival did not reach significance (HR 0.80, 0.61–1.04, p=0.088), the analysis was taken at 179 deaths against 285 planned events, the R1 subgroup showed nothing (HR 1.04, 0.57–1.92), the trial was conducted only in Japan and S-1 is unavailable in the United States.

alt.t: After an R1 resection, discuss adjuvant chemoradiation in addition to systemic therapy as a shared decision, weighing toxicity against local-recurrence benefit.
alt.pref: A microscopically positive margin, with radiation oncology review of margins, nodal burden and toxicity. Local recurrence is the failure pattern radiation can address, and R1 resection is common in this disease — AASLD reports up to 50% of cases.
alt.avoid: NCCN lists an option; it does not make this mandatory for every R1 case. The supporting data are retrospective meta-analyses — BSG cites 21 retrospective studies and more than 1,400 patients — plus the single-arm SWOG S0809 phase II trial (2-year survival 67% after R0 and 60% after R1), which this depot carries only as quoted by BSG and not as a primary paper. The Milan consensus states flatly that adjuvant radiotherapy remains unproven, with benefit suggested mainly in R1 and N1 disease.
alt.note: Whether node-positive R0 disease should prompt the same discussion is open (§11 item 10): NCCN places nodal involvement alongside margin status as a trigger, BSG limits its recommendation to R1 resection, and the node-positive benefit rests on retrospective meta-analysis.

avoid.t: Adjuvant gemcitabine after resection of bile duct cancer.
avoid.pref: Nothing in this disease — use capecitabine if adjuvant treatment is given. This is the one adjuvant randomised trial confined to the population this page covers, which is why it carries weight here despite its size.
avoid.avoid: BCAT (n=225, perihilar and distal bile duct cancer only, no intrahepatic and no gallbladder disease) was null: median overall survival 62.3 versus 63.8 months, hazard ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.70–1.45), p=0.964, with no subgroup benefiting, including node-positive and R1 patients, and grade 3–4 neutropenia in 58.4% versus 3.8%.
avoid.note: Read the null honestly in both directions. Recruitment stopped at 226 of a planned 300 because most patients wanted adjuvant chemotherapy, and the authors calculate only a 2.8% probability the result would have reached significance even with the planned 189 deaths. Observed 5-year survival was about 50% against an assumed 30%, because R2 resections, distant metastases, severe surgical complications and in-hospital deaths were all excluded — a favourable cohort with too few events. This rules out gemcitabine, not adjuvant therapy.

avoid.avoid: PRODIGE-12 was negative on both co-primary endpoints — relapse-free survival 30.4 versus 18.5 months, HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.62–1.25), p=0.48, and time to definitive deterioration of global quality of life 31.8 versus 32.1 months, HR 1.28 (0.73–2.26) — and overall survival numerically favoured surveillance (HR 1.08, 0.70–1.66). Worst adverse event was grade 3 in 62% and grade 4 in 11%, the 73% figure the roadmap quotes.
avoid.note: Both medians fell on a plateau of the survival curves, so the 30.4 versus 18.5 month gap overstates the separation; the authors say the hazard ratio is the honest summary. The population was lower risk than BILCAP (13% R1, 38% node-positive) and only 28% had extrahepatic disease.

avoid.t: Resection attempted without drainage of the future liver remnant.
avoid.pref: Drain the remnant, confirm the bilirubin is falling within 1–2 weeks, and only then proceed.
avoid.avoid: This is the roadmap's named Avoid for Gate 1 and it is a sequence error, not a judgement call.

gates.name: 4 · Transplant protocol candidate
crit: Unresectable for technical reasons or because of underlying liver disease, or arising in primary sclerosing cholangitis
If a mass is present, a single mass under 3 cm in radial diameter — longitudinal duct extension is not the measured criterion
No intrahepatic or extrahepatic metastases on chest and abdominal imaging within 90 days of the initial request, and no regional nodal disease
Confirmed malignancy, and no transperitoneal biopsy of the primary tumour
A centre holding an OPTN-committee-approved written patient-care protocol, with operative staging before transplantation
gates.ask: Has the transplant question been asked and answered before anything forecloses it?

standard.t: Ask this gate before starting palliative systemic therapy — months of chemotherapy, or a transperitoneal biopsy obtained for convenience, commonly forecloses it.
standard.pref: Every unresectable perihilar patient who is small-volume, node-negative and medically transplantable, and every patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis. The protocol population is defined by being unresectable and small.
standard.avoid: The sequencing recommendation rests on protocol eligibility criteria, not on a randomised comparison of referral timing — that trial does not exist.
standard.note: AASLD goes further than the roadmap and states that transplantation is preferred over resection in all cases of primary sclerosing cholangitis, but that document is expert consensus rather than a GRADE-rated guideline. The 12-centre series found no difference in outcome by PSC status, so the PSC preference is not a finding of the primary data. Whether PSC-associated tumours should be routed here even when technically resectable is an open local decision (alignment area 9).

alt.t: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by staging laparotomy and liver transplantation, under a written protocol with registry entry.
alt.pref: A protocol candidate meeting every policy condition at a programme that holds the approval. In 287 patients across 12 US centres, intention-to-treat survival from the start of therapy was 68% at 2 years and 53% at 5 years. The recurrence-free survival figures quoted elsewhere are on a different and smaller denominator: 78% at 2 years (95% CI 72–84), 65% at 5 years (57–73) and 59% at 10 years among the 214 who reached transplantation, with graft survival 77%, 60% and 51%. Keep the two apart — 53% at 5 years is what the pathway delivers to a patient who enters it, 65% is what it delivers to a patient who gets through it.
alt.avoid: Do not read these as a treatment effect. The experience is retrospective and multicentre with no arm of transplantation without neoadjuvant therapy and none of resection, so the benefit credited to chemoradiation is inferred from historical recurrence rates; 193 of 287 patients (67%) came from one centre; neoadjuvant protocols differed widely between centres (brachytherapy in 75%, maintenance chemotherapy in 65%, external beam dose 2,100–6,000 cGy), and that heterogeneity meant the independent effect of maintenance chemotherapy could not be determined. Selection is doing substantial work: patients transplanted outside criteria did significantly worse (HR 2.98, 95% CI 1.79–4.95, P<.001) and selection was the only independent predictor of recurrence-free survival. 71 of 287 (25%) dropped out at a median of 4.6 months, a rate averaging 11.5% per 3-month interval from the end of chemoradiation (range 7–17%). Staging surgery still found metastases in 17% (40 of 229), though with only 30 transplanted patients unstaged that comparison was underpowered (HR 0.73, 0.37–1.43).
alt.note: Two further honesty points about the denominator. 15 patients (5%) were transplanted on clinical suspicion alone with no histologic proof of malignancy; excluding them, 5-year intention-to-treat survival was 50% and recurrence-free survival 62% — little changed, but it means the cohort includes patients who may not have had cancer. And the widely quoted 5-year figures of 55–65% in primary sclerosing cholangitis and 35–55% in de novo disease are an ungraded 2015 consensus statement, not a result of this series, which found no difference by PSC status; do not quote them as outcomes of the protocol. Toxicity is real: radiation caused portal vein friability in 23% and hepatic artery friability in 12%, gastroduodenal ulcers in 34%, biliary anastomotic strictures in 17%, ischaemic cholangiopathy in 7%, postsurgical bile leak in 11%, and 22 of 214 (10%) needed re-transplantation, 11 of them for arterial compromise. The regimen is typically 4500 cGy external beam in 30 fractions with 5-FU, a 1500–3000 cGy brachytherapy boost, then capecitabine until transplant. [TX-TIMING] [PAYER]

alt.t: Radiotherapy, sometimes SBRT in a centre-specific protocol, may contribute to a curative transplant strategy — as a component of the approved regimen, not as a substitute for it.
alt.pref: Discuss the transplant protocol before any radiation is planned. The evidence supports the whole neoadjuvant-plus-transplant pathway, not radiation alone.
alt.avoid: Do not substitute an arbitrary SBRT schedule for approved neoadjuvant treatment, and do not assume it confers allocation eligibility. Isolated SBRT cure evidence is limited, and central bile duct, duodenal and infection risks can require a different fractionation.
alt.note: A local complete response is not an automatic transplant exception. Record bridge or downstaging treatment separately from definitive local treatment. Graded D: no study in this depot isolates the contribution of radiotherapy within the protocol, and the ESMO guideline grades external beam radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy as definitive treatment of locally advanced disease [II, D], to be used only in trials.

avoid.t: Starting palliative systemic therapy in a potentially protocol-eligible patient before the transplant question has been asked and answered.
avoid.pref: Route the case through the transplant surgeon at the first board, together with the drainage plan.
avoid.avoid: This is the roadmap's named Avoid for Gate 2, and the commonest way the option is lost.

avoid.t: Do not use Rea 2005 to tell a resectable patient that transplantation is the better operation.
avoid.pref: The defensible claim from that paper is what the Mayo protocol achieves in a selected, node-negative, mostly PSC population — not that transplantation beats resection in a patient who is resectable.
avoid.avoid: The selection asymmetry is complete and the authors say so. By protocol no transplant patient was resectable, and every recipient was proved node-negative at staging laparotomy, while 8 of 26 resected patients (31%) were node-positive and 3 of 26 (12%) R1. The curves also start at different points: 82% 5-year survival is measured from transplantation among the 38 of 71 enrolled who got there, against 21% from resection among the 26 of 54 explored; from the start of treatment the comparison is 58% versus about 21%. Recipients were 15 years younger (48 versus 63, P<0.001) and 58% had PSC against 8%. 16 of 38 explants showed no residual tumour and 8 of those patients had no tissue proof of cancer before neoadjuvant therapy.
avoid.note: The node-negative R0 resection subgroup fared no better (87%, 53% and 18% at 1, 3 and 5 years), and the 20–21% 5-year survival after resection matches other specialist centres, so the comparator is not substandard. Three of 26 resections (12%) died within 30 days, and the discussants' point was that non-cancer deaths, not recurrence, drive much of the gap — recurrence after resection was 35% while 5-year survival was 20%. There is no intention-to-treat analysis and no accounting of organ cost: 38 grafts, 7 of them living donor, for 71 patients enrolled. The Milan jury acknowledged benefit in node-negative patients independent of resectability; that is a consensus position resting on one benchmark study and mixed retrospective comparisons, and TRANSPHIL, the randomised trial meant to settle it, failed to recruit.

avoid.t: Do not treat the transplant eligibility criteria as clinical thresholds that can be stretched for a good candidate.
avoid.pref: They are conditions of OPTN Policy 9.5.A, not entry criteria of the 12-centre series, which transplanted 48 patients outside them. Exactly 3 cm does not meet the policy mass-size gate; referral and allocation are distinct, and NCCN's ≤3 cm referral wording is looser than the policy.
avoid.avoid: Mass size caused the greatest disparity in the multicentre series: 5-year recurrence-free survival was 32% for a mass over 3 cm against 69% for 3 cm or smaller (P<.001).
avoid.note: Confirm the current OPTN policy text before any listing decision. The transplant coordinator records source version, eligibility dates, request and extension dates, imaging, laboratory values and a named renewal owner; transplant leadership signs the allocation assessment.

gates.name: 5 · Unresectable outside the protocol
crit: Regional nodal disease, or a mass of 3 cm or more in radial diameter
Intrahepatic or extrahepatic metastases
Comorbidity or performance status that rules out transplantation
No OPTN-approved protocol available, or the patient declines that route
gates.ask: What is the best systemic plan, and is the biliary tree drained well enough to deliver it?

opts.name: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus durvalumab
opts.when: NCCN and ESMO both recommend it first line; ESMO's interim update grades the two checkpoint combinations [I, A] together.
opts.pref: A fit patient with adequate drainage and an acceptable bilirubin. TOPAZ-1 (n=685) gave overall survival hazard ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.66–0.97), P=0.021, median 12.8 versus 11.5 months, with the separation in the tail — 24-month survival 24.9% versus 10.4%, and a hazard ratio of 0.91 (0.66–1.26) in the first 6 months against 0.74 (0.58–0.94) thereafter.
opts.avoid: Address biliary infection and organ reserve before starting; prior immune exposure changes later choices. No trial compares durvalumab with pembrolizumab, and no clinical, biochemical or molecular biomarker favours one over the other — ESMO's statement that they are interchangeable is an indirect comparison across two trials that differ in chemotherapy duration and population. This was a prespecified interim analysis at 424 of 496 planned deaths powered to about 75%, the median gain is 1.3 months, and the proportional hazards assumption was formally violated, so a single hazard ratio misrepresents a time-varying effect.

opts.name: Cisplatin–gemcitabine plus pembrolizumab
opts.when: Recommended first line alongside the durvalumab combination, unranked.
opts.pref: The same population. KEYNOTE-966 (n=1,069) gave median overall survival 12.7 versus 10.9 months, hazard ratio 0.83 (95% CI 0.72–0.95); 24-month survival 25% versus 18%.
opts.avoid: Both supporting endpoints failed their prespecified boundaries — progression-free survival HR 0.86 (0.75–1.00), p=0.023 against 0.0125, and objective response identical at 29% versus 29%, p=0.47 — so the benefit rests on one endpoint with no response signal behind it. More importantly for this page: the trial was enriched for intrahepatic disease (59%) because tumour tissue was mandatory, and the extrahepatic subgroup, which is where perihilar tumours sit, gave an overall survival hazard ratio of 0.99 (95% CI 0.73–1.35). Immune-mediated events occurred in 22% versus 13% and treatment-related deaths in 8 (2%) versus 3 (1%), with no improvement in quality of life.

standard.order: Downgraded from A to B for this page, and the reason is subgroup, not design: both trials are properly conducted positive phase 3 trials in biliary tract cancer as a whole, but neither was powered for perihilar disease, and in the one that reported it the extrahepatic subgroup hazard ratio was 0.99 (0.73–1.35). The order carries no meaning: NCCN lists both, ESMO grades both [I, A], and no trial compares them. The backbone is cisplatin–gemcitabine, which established the standard in ABC-02 (n=410: median overall survival 11.7 versus 8.1 months, hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52–0.80); 57 of those 410 patients had hilar tumours and no differential effect by site was seen, but the trial was not powered to find one.
standard.flagnote: The roadmap retains an unranked choice between the two combinations; that is the institutional position and it matches NCCN and ESMO. New ratification question (§11 item 12): is first-line chemo-immunotherapy offered here on the biliary-tract-wide result, given the null extrahepatic subgroup in KEYNOTE-966 and the absence of a perihilar-specific estimate in either trial?

standard.t: Order molecular profiling at diagnosis and screen for clinical-trial eligibility at the same visit.
standard.pref: Every patient entering systemic therapy. Actionable alterations do occur in perihilar disease, but not in the same pattern as intrahepatic disease. FGFR2 fusions and IDH1 mutations concentrate in intrahepatic tumours — ClarIDHy enrolled 187 patients of whom only 6 had extrahepatic or perihilar disease, and FIGHT-202 cohort A was 107 of 108 intrahepatic — while HER2 alterations occur in about 5–10% of biliary tract cancer and are commoner in extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma, which makes HER2 the one target enriched in this disease rather than depleted.
standard.avoid: Do not assume hilar disease shares the iCCA target distribution, and do not treat the gene as the target — different alterations in the same gene do not predict the same response, as ESMO notes for HER2 amplification versus mutation. ESMO also concedes there are no standardised criteria for assessing HER2 status in biliary tract cancer and that no specific test can be recommended, with gastric cancer immunohistochemistry criteria offered as the best available; two HER2-directed recommendations then rest on that undefined assay.
standard.note: Downgraded from A to B. Profiling itself is graded [I, A] by ESMO, but almost every therapeutic recommendation that follows from it is level III, grade A — single-arm phase II or basket-trial evidence with no randomised comparator — and several named agents are FDA- but not EMA-approved. Use the source edition's full actionable panel, including NRG1 where appropriate. Preserve tissue for it; next-generation sequencing of the ERCP specimen can serve both diagnosis and target identification, and in the 6-year multi-institutional series it found actionable alterations in 30% of cholangiocarcinomas.

standard.t: Durable biliary drainage is a co-primary goal of treatment, not supportive care around it.
standard.pref: Recurrent cholangitis, not tumour progression, is often what ends treatment. Adequate drainage and an acceptable bilirubin come before the first cycle, and new jaundice or fever goes down the urgent lane rather than waiting for the next scan.
standard.avoid: Do not deliver liver-directed therapy without relieving obstruction first.

alt.t: Radiotherapy for local control or symptoms, including definitive chemoradiation for selected localised unresectable disease.
alt.pref: Local symptoms, or localised unresectable disease where the goal is control rather than cure.
alt.avoid: Avoid radiotherapy that would compromise later protocol eligibility in a patient still under transplant consideration. Isolated SBRT cure evidence is limited, and central bile duct, duodenal and infection risks can require a different fractionation.
alt.note: Graded D: no study in this depot supports definitive chemoradiation in perihilar disease, the AHPBA panel's figure for definitive chemoradiation in unresectable patients ineligible for transplant is a median survival of 10.7–14.6 months from uncontrolled series, and ESMO grades external beam radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy as definitive treatment of locally advanced cholangiocarcinoma [II, D] — not to be used outside trials.

alt.t: Second line, FOLFOX after progression on a platinum doublet.
alt.pref: A patient who has kept performance status and wants further treatment. ABC-06 (n=162) gave median overall survival 6.2 versus 5.3 months against active symptom control, adjusted hazard ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.97), p=0.031; 6-month survival 50.6% versus 35.5% and 12-month survival 25.9% versus 11.4%.
alt.avoid: The absolute gain is 0.9 months of median survival, with grade 3–5 events in 69% versus 52% and three chemotherapy-related deaths. Objective response was seen in only 4 of 81 patients (5%), so the benefit is disease stabilisation, not shrinkage. More patients in the FOLFOX arm were platinum resistant or refractory (67% versus 58%), an imbalance in a factor that was itself independently prognostic, and stratification errors found during data cleaning required a post-hoc sensitivity analysis (adjusted HR 0.68, 0.49–0.95). Say both halves out loud.

alt.t: Where a driver is present, use the agent matched to that specific alteration.
alt.pref: FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, IDH1 mutation, BRAF V600E, HER2 overexpression (IHC 3+), MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficiency, and rare targetable fusions can all occur in this disease.
alt.avoid: Except for IDH1, these are single-arm response data rather than comparative survival data, and the matched-therapy trials enrolled almost only intrahepatic tumours — FIGHT-202 cohort A 107 of 108 intrahepatic, FOENIX-CCA2 intrahepatic only, ROAR 39 of 43 (91%) intrahepatic, ClarIDHy 6 of 187 extrahepatic or perihilar — so their effect in perihilar disease is an extrapolation. Every one of these trials was industry sponsored with company employees among the authors, and all of them are second-line or later, so none says anything about conversion to resection. HER2 is the exception worth pursuing here, because it is enriched in extrahepatic disease: in HERIZON-BTC-01 zanidatamab gave a confirmed response rate of 41% overall but 52% (39–65) in immunohistochemistry 3+ tumours against 6% (1 of 18) in 2+, with median overall survival 18.1 versus 5.2 months — so the 3+ restriction is doing the work, and the trial reports no breakdown by anatomical subsite.
alt.note: Even the randomised case is partial: in ClarIDHy ivosidenib improved progression-free survival (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.25–0.54) but the intention-to-treat overall-survival difference was not significant (median 10.3 versus 7.5 months, HR 0.79, 0.56–1.12, one-sided P=.09), significance appearing only after a rank-preserving structural failure time adjustment for the 70% of placebo patients who crossed over; objective response was 2%, the comparator was placebo rather than second-line FOLFOX, and the agent will not convert unresectable disease to resectable. No randomised evidence sequences the targeted options.

avoid.t: Thermal ablation of the perihilar primary.
avoid.pref: Resection, or protocol neoadjuvant therapy followed by transplantation, should be considered first where the patient is eligible. Graded D: this is a position taken on the absence of evidence in central biliary tumours, not on a comparative study.
avoid.avoid: Not an established curative option. Central biliary and vascular anatomy and longitudinal tumour spread differ from a small peripheral liver mass, so iCCA ablation selection rules do not transfer. Endobiliary ablation to improve drainage is a different procedure and does not establish cure.

avoid.t: Y90 radioembolisation or TACE for the hilar primary.
avoid.pref: No standard first- or second-line role for the primary, and graded D because no study in this depot addresses a central perihilar primary. A peripheral intrahepatic recurrence or metastatic target may occasionally be discussed for hepatic control, but that is a different indication and is not the iCCA pathway; in exceptional liver-dominant recurrent disease, use only a specific multidisciplinary rationale or a trial.
avoid.avoid: Neither is established for curative treatment of a central perihilar primary. Drainage, infection risk and arterial coverage require expert assessment, and prior drainage or instrumentation increases infectious risk.

avoid.t: Hepatic arterial infusion for the hilar primary, outside a disease-specific trial.
avoid.pref: Research or exceptional use with an explicit control goal; standard systemic therapy remains the backbone outside curative pathways.
avoid.avoid: The principal HAI studies are in unresectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma — the phase II trial of HAI floxuridine with systemic gemcitabine–oxaliplatin treated 38 of 84 screened patients with liver-confined iCCA and met its 6-month progression-free survival endpoint at 84.1%, with median overall survival 25.0 months against a historical comparator — and they cannot justify a routine hilar-primary pathway. That trial was single-arm and single-institution, 11% of patients had grade 4 pump or arterial complications and 30% did so in the 10-patient confirmatory cohort, and 11% needed biliary stents, two of them for chemotherapy-induced biliary sclerosis. In a tumour whose problem is central biliary obstruction, that last figure is the relevant one.
avoid.note: Graded D for this page: the evidence is in a different anatomical disease, and the toxicity that matters most here — biliary sclerosis — is the one the iCCA trial reports.

avoid.t: Histotripsy, outside a prospective trial or institutional registry.
avoid.pref: The roadmap's label here is trial or prospective registry only, with explicit consent about oncologic uncertainty, suitable ultrasound visibility and acoustic access, device-compliant target size and depth, and an independent standard-treatment review. Graded D: there is no perihilar evidence at all.
avoid.avoid: No tumour-specific curative evidence. FDA device clearance for tumour destruction does not establish survival benefit or equivalence to established ablation; in the one-year HOPE4LIVER update of 47 patients and 52 tumours, local control was 63.4% on the primary assessment against 90% post hoc. A bridge-to-transplant use remains protocol-based, and a technical response does not establish transplant eligibility. Studies must address hilar anatomy, drainage and transplant consequences explicitly.

gates.name: 6 · Best supportive care
crit: Poor performance status that is not explained by jaundice or sepsis
Uncontrolled sepsis
Patient choice
gates.ask: Is anything I can offer going to help this patient, and has drainage been given its chance first?

standard.t: Effective drainage, pruritus and pain control, nutritional support, and early specialist palliative involvement.
standard.pref: Every patient at this gate, and alongside antitumour treatment at the earlier ones. Effective drainage is part of supportive care, not an alternative to it.
standard.avoid: Do not let a decision for supportive care become a decision against drainage — a blocked, infected biliary tree is the commonest reversible cause of the state that put the patient here.
standard.note: Downgraded from A to C, because the package is not one intervention and only part of it has evidence in this depot. Drainage rests on guideline recommendations graded low to very low quality; early specialist palliative involvement rests on trial evidence in other cancers that this reference depot does not contain; pruritus control, pain control and nutritional support are uncontroversial but untested here. The grade should not be read as though a trial had tested the bundle.

alt.t: If jaundice and sepsis are driving performance status, re-evaluate after drainage before assigning this gate.
alt.pref: The acutely unwell, newly presenting patient. This reverses more often than expected.
alt.avoid: Do not assign the gate on a performance status measured during cholangitis.

avoid.t: Antitumour therapy without realistic benefit, and repeat interventions that cannot change the plan.
avoid.pref: One recommendation, one owner, one reassessment date — and a documented alternative considered.
avoid.avoid: Repeating a procedure because it is the procedure that was done last time. After progression or toxicity, restage and reconsider the whole treatment rather than automatically repeating the same intervention.
avoid.note: Graded D: an operating rule the programme has chosen, not a comparative result. Audit it for adherence, not for effectiveness.

Type IV — secondary ducts involved bilaterally
Hepatectomy with transplantation in the original series, on 3 patients, one of whom recurred in the hepatic pedicle at 8 months; the Milan consensus favours left trisectionectomy
quickref.foot: Caudate resection is obligatory from type II upward because the ducts draining segment 1 are almost always involved; large type II or IIIa tumours may also need resection of segment 4. All five type II and IIIa patients treated by local excision alone had involved margins and recurred locally. Read the classification with its limits: the type-specific plan rests on 23 resections accumulated over 30 years at one centre, one to four patients per type, with imaging, staging and technique changing throughout and no comparison group. Only 19 of 122 operated patients (15.6%) had a macroscopically curative resection and only 9 of 122 (7.4%) a histologically negative margin. The series shows its own classification understates extent — 4 operative type IV tumours became 9 on histology. The type-IV transplantation recommendation predates portal vein embolisation, remnant volumetry and the Mayo neoadjuvant protocol. The Milan jury declined to endorse Bismuth-Corlette, or any staging system including MSKCC, as a predictor of resectability, and its own resectability criteria are stated to be expert opinion requiring validation; the roadmap says the type does not by itself determine resectability: vascular involvement, lobar atrophy, nodal status and remnant volume do.

Prior abdominal radiation, a previous resection attempt violating the tumour plane and another malignancy within 5 years are exclusions in the published protocol and in AASLD. An MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15 under Policy 9.4.E; a candidate registered between 12 and 18 is assigned MMaT rather than MMaT-3, so confirm the route for anyone listed before adulthood. Outcome context, with the denominators kept apart: in 287 patients across 12 US centres intention-to-treat survival from the start of therapy was 68% at 2 years and 53% at 5 years, while recurrence-free survival of 78% at 2 years and 65% at 5 years is measured among the 214 who reached transplantation, and graft survival among those was 77% and 60%. Excluding the 15 patients (5%) transplanted on clinical suspicion with no histologic proof, 5-year intention-to-treat survival was 50% and recurrence-free survival 62%. Patients transplanted outside these criteria did significantly worse (hazard ratio 2.98, 95% CI 1.79–4.95), with mass size the largest single disparity (5-year recurrence-free survival 32% for a mass over 3 cm versus 69% for 3 cm or smaller); that hazard ratio is for the composite off-criteria group and is not attributable to any one violation. 71 of 287 (25%) dropped out at a median of 4.6 months, averaging 11.5% per 3-month interval (range 7–17%), and 67% of the cohort came from one centre. The frequently quoted 5-year figures of 55–65% in PSC and 35–55% de novo are a 2015 consensus statement, not a result of this series, which found no difference by PSC status. Verify the current OPTN policy text before any listing decision.

quickref.title: Drainage targets, and the route question
quickref.intro: What to drain, how much of it, and what the randomised comparison of routes actually showed.
rows: Which sectors
Those forming the future liver remnant; generally not atrophic segments
Is drainage routine?

No. ESGE 2026 suggests against routine preoperative drainage and accepts severe jaundice, cholangitis or a predicted remnant of 30% or less; the Coelen investigators add that it may be unnecessary when the remnant exceeds 50%
Volume target in palliative drainage
More than 50% of viable liver volume including the future liver remnant (NCCN); ESGE 2026 adds ideally 70% or more. No threshold has been derived — grade D
Sector volumes for planning
Right anterior, right posterior and left about 30% each; segments I and IV about 10%; atrophic segments count as non-viable
Stents by Bismuth type
Types I, II and IIIb can often be served by one stent in the right main hepatic duct; IIIa and IV need two or more to reach 50%
Bilateral or unilateral stent

Unsettled, and the page takes no position: ASGE suggests bilateral absent atrophy on a pooled survival gain of 11 days (95% CI −12 to 35) and no pooled patency difference; one randomised trial favours bilateral on patency (252 versus 139 days)
How many drains
As few as achieve remnant decompression, with one named owner for the strategy
Bilirubin threshold before major hepatectomy, embolic therapy, radiation or systemic therapy
A programme threshold, not an evidence threshold — set locally, recorded, applied consistently
Route
Unsettled; an anatomy and expertise decision
quickref.foot: The randomised comparison in resectable perihilar disease (DRAINAGE, 54 of a planned 106 patients, 70% Bismuth IIIa, IIIb or IV) was negative on its primary endpoint: one or more severe drainage-related complications in 17 of 27 (63%) after percutaneous drainage versus 18 of 27 (67%) after endoscopic drainage, relative risk 0.94 (95% CI 0.64–1.40), with no difference in the number per patient. It was stopped early because mortality between randomisation and 90 days after surgery was higher after percutaneous drainage: 11 of 27 (41%) versus 3 of 27 (11%), relative risk 3.67 (95% CI 1.15–11.69), p=0.03, cause never identified, the trial underpowered, and the authors themselves calling the signal prone to type I error. Read it against its own context: 90-day all-cause mortality in the trial was 26% overall against 10% among 100 contemporaneous patients with presumed resectable disease at the same four centres, so neither figure is the expected risk of either route; a third of patients entered after a failed stenting attempt elsewhere; and the 16 patients who received both routes had the best outcomes. Technical success favoured the percutaneous route (93% versus 74%) and 15 of 27 endoscopic patients (56%) crossed over to percutaneous against 1 of 27 the other way, so the trial compares initial strategies rather than techniques. Pooled across three randomised trials, ASGE found 30-day mortality only trending lower with endoscopic drainage (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.28–1.01, p=0.05), with lower technical success (OR 0.21), far more crossover (OR 18.2) and more pancreatitis (OR 3.69) in the endoscopic arm. ESGE 2026 nonetheless recommends ERCP over percutaneous drainage preoperatively (strong, moderate quality), and a 1,085-patient meta-analysis found more implantation metastases after the percutaneous route (OR 0.35, 0.23–0.53) — while ESGE's own section cites a meta-analysis giving percutaneous drainage higher therapeutic success (OR 3.5, 2.1–6.0) and 11.5-fold more reintervention after ERCP, with 10 of 11 studies retrospective. What is not optional is draining the correct sectors.

quickref.intro: For the discussion about how hard to push for tissue, and which route can be used at all.

Pooled sensitivity 0.66 (ASGE), incremental yield over brushing 20% (9–31); separately, mean sensitivity 49%, specificity 96%, negative predictive value 34% (SD 24.63) in a 294-patient meta-analysis at 77% pretest probability
