Cholangioscopy-guided targeted biopsy

Pooled 65% (95% CI 35–87) from 4 studies and 128 PSC patients; 15% (0–31) in a real-world cohort of 80 where 88% had had a prior ERCP, 55% had a stent removed at the procedure, 40% had PSC and a median of 3 biopsies were taken with 33% inconclusive — and where brush cytology at the same procedure did better (47%, specificity 95%)
FISH polysomy, in PSC

Sensitivity 51% (43–59), specificity 93% (91–95), positive predictive value 0.68; trisomy or tetrasomy alone uninformative (31%, 71%, positive likelihood ratio 1.19). All 8 pooled studies came from one centre with overlapping cohorts
Cytological criteria on a brushing

3 or more of 11 malignant characteristics gives sensitivity 70%, specificity 97%; 7 of 30 malignant brushings showed none of them, and necrosis and infiltrating inflammation do not distinguish malignancy
Next-generation sequencing of ERCP-obtained specimens
82% sensitivity, 98% specificity on 1,979 patients with follow-up, against 44% and 99% for pathology on separate specimens; 80% versus 36% in intrahepatic or hilar strictures
Sequencing plus pathology

88% sensitivity at 97% specificity; 86% in intrahepatic or hilar strictures. In the one real-world cohort reporting it, the gain in cholangiocarcinoma itself was not significant (70% versus 60%, P=.72)
quickref.foot: With either conventional modality a negative result does not exclude malignancy: negative predictive values were 34% and 47% in a meta-analysis of 294 patients at a pretest probability of 77%, with standard deviations as large as the estimates, so repeated sampling in pursuit of a negative that will not be believed is a common way to lose time. That pooled ERCP-versus-EUS comparison is not specific to perihilar disease — where the primary may be small, periductal-infiltrating and a poor aspiration target — only 3 of its 8 studies applied both tests to the same patients, three of its proximal-stricture studies enrolled patients only after ERCP sampling had already failed, and QUADAS-2 scored every study at high risk of selection bias. The sequencing endpoint in the multi-institutional study was a neoplastic stricture, which is broader than malignancy, a stricture could be classified neoplastic on 12 months of imaging and clinical progression rather than on tissue, identical specimens were never compared, FISH was never compared head to head, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. A negative sequencing result is not reassuring either: negative predictive value was 63% in the developer's prospective series (37 false negatives, 25%) and 74–82% in one real-world cohort. Real-world cohorts reproduce the direction of effect (65% versus 52% alone and 78% combined on 47 biopsies in one; 75% versus 42.9% in 77 patients in the other) but not the primary sclerosing cholangitis result: against 83% versus 8% on 12 malignant cases in the developer's series, and 85% versus 26% on 89 neoplastic strictures in the larger multi-institutional study, one real-world cohort found 20% sensitivity in PSC, worse than brush cytology at 40%. Cholangioscopy is not harm-free: 11% post-procedure cholangitis and 15% procedural failure in PSC ducts, and adverse events in 13% of the real-world cohort including one cardiac arrest. Whether a molecular result satisfies the transplant protocol's confirmed-malignancy condition is an undecided local question.

honest.t: Which sectors are drained? Those forming the future liver remnant. This requires the operative plan to exist before the drainage plan, which is why Gate 0 and Gate 1 are discussed together at the first tumour board.
honest.why: Grade D. No trial tests remnant-focused drainage against draining the most accessible duct. The position follows from the physiology of hypertrophy in a cholestatic liver and from a local failure pattern, not from comparative outcome data.

honest.t: How many drains? As few as achieve remnant decompression. Multiple uncoordinated drains placed by different services is a recognised failure pattern; one named owner manages the drainage strategy.
honest.why: Grade D. An operating rule, not a comparative result. Audited as drains per patient and cholangitis episodes (§11 item 7).

honest.t: When is bilirubin low enough? A programme threshold, not an evidence threshold. Set it locally, record it, and apply it consistently before major hepatectomy, embolic therapy, radiation, and systemic therapy.
honest.why: Grade D. No comparative data define the cut-off; it is a safety convention. §11 item 3 audits post-hepatectomy liver failure by preoperative bilirubin so the local number can eventually be defended.

honest.t: Nodal assessment is a different act. EUS evaluation of regional nodes, including aspiration of a suspicious node, addresses a different question from biopsying the primary. Node-positive disease is itself a protocol exclusion, so a positive nodal result does not cost candidacy that existed — it identifies a patient who was never a candidate, before a transplant workup is spent.
honest.why: Grade D. The logic is sound but untested, and AASLD notes there are no clearly identified morphological criteria for a malignant node, which weakens any 'suspicious node' trigger. AASLD requires EUS-FNA of regional nodes in every transplant candidate before neoadjuvant therapy; the roadmap is looser and limits it to suspicious nodes (§11, alignment area 8).

honest.t: If a stent is already in place, do not treat a negative result as reassuring — and do not assume cholangioscopic sampling beats a brush taken after the stent comes out.
honest.why: Local consensus, grade D, and the draft's earlier wording has been withdrawn. No study quantifies sampling yield stratified by prior stent placement in biliary strictures; targeted searches for it return nothing. The one real-world cohort that tested both found the opposite of the draft's assumption: cholangioscopy-guided biopsy was 15% sensitive while brush cytology at the same procedure was 47% sensitive with 95% specificity and a diagnostic odds ratio of 19.6 against 6.6. In that cohort 55% had a plastic stent removed at the start of the procedure, 40% had PSC, a median of 3 biopsies were taken with 33% inconclusive, and 66 of 80 procedures used a first-generation device — so the low figure is as much about sampling technique and population as about the stent, and the authors' own remedy is at least four biopsies, not a different instrument.

honest.t: Is molecular testing more robust after stenting? Mechanistically it should be, because sequencing detects tumour-specific alterations rather than interpreting morphology, so reactive atypia has no obvious route to a false positive.
honest.why: Mechanism only — not demonstrated. None of the sequencing studies report performance stratified by prior stenting, so this is reasoning, not data. A countervailing concern also has no data: an inflamed, stented duct may shed more non-neoplastic epithelium and dilute the tumour fraction.

honest.t: Resection may proceed on imaging plus the clinical picture where the operative plan would not change. A malignant-appearing stricture with no alternative explanation is treated as cancer.
honest.why: Grade C, and concordant with NCCN and BSG — but it means a benign aetiology is found in about 10% of resections done on a presumptive diagnosis by the AHPBA panel's figure and about 15% in a 30-year tertiary series, in an operation whose 90-day mortality reaches 13% and whose severe-complication rate reaches 70% even in benchmark patients at expert centres. BSG also carries this as a STRONG recommendation resting on LOW-quality evidence.

honest.t: Transperitoneal biopsy of the primary must be avoided in any patient who may be protocol-eligible. Whether the same constraint should extend to resection-only candidates is a genuine local decision and is unresolved.
honest.why: The avoidance rule for protocol candidates is a policy condition, not a weighing of evidence, and needs no vote. The scope question does: the roadmap's §4 Resection row says the route is unconstrained, while its own ESGE callout says not to pass a needle toward a perihilar tumour in any patient who still has a curative option, which includes resection. BSG states the stricter rule, and a resection candidate judged unresectable before any operative violation of the tumour plane may become a protocol candidate.

honest.t: The transplant pathway rests on retrospective multicentre protocol experience, not randomised comparison; its eligibility criteria are protocol conditions, not evidence-based thresholds.
honest.why: The roadmap states this about its own §6. There is no arm of transplantation without neoadjuvant therapy and no randomised comparison with resection, the authors of the multicentre series argue such a trial is now unethical, and 67% of its patients came from one centre. Graft stewardship is an institutional judgement (§11 item 1).

honest.t: The tumour board operating model is reproduced unchanged across every disease roadmap so the programme has one operating standard rather than five. It is evidence grade D by construction and is labelled Standard because the programme has chosen it, not because trials support it. Audit it for adherence, not for effectiveness.
honest.why: The roadmap says so in §10. These are stakeholder-derived operating requirements.

honest.t: A minimum annual volume for extended hepatectomy with biliary reconstruction at this centre has not been set.
honest.why: Volume-outcome relationships in this operation are observational but consistent; the threshold itself is a governance choice, not a measurable one (§11 item 4). [EXPERTISE]

honest.t: Gate 0 is named 'Biliary drainage comes first', and that is a sequencing rule, not an indication. ESGE 2026 suggests against routine preoperative drainage in malignant hilar obstruction.
honest.why: The guidelines accept drainage for severe jaundice, cholangitis or a predicted remnant of 30% or less; the Milan consensus restricts it to a small remnant needing hypertrophy, cholangitis, renal or hepatic failure, severe malnutrition or pruritus; and the Coelen investigators' own conclusion was that drainage should follow resectability assessment and may be unnecessary when the remnant exceeds 50% of liver volume. The Asia-Pacific panel reached only 56% full agreement on its own preoperative-drainage statement. What Gate 0 establishes is that if you drain, you drain the remnant and you do it before anything that depends on hypertrophy — not that every jaundiced patient is drained.

honest.t: The drainage-route position is weaker than its grade suggested, and the page has been downgraded from B to C.
honest.why: The only randomised comparison was negative on its primary endpoint — severe drainage-related complications 63% after percutaneous versus 67% after endoscopic drainage, relative risk 0.94 (0.64–1.40) — and was stopped at 54 of a planned 106 patients for a mortality difference whose cause the safety board never identified and which the authors call prone to type I error. Pooled across three trials, 30-day mortality only trended lower with endoscopic drainage (RR 0.53, 0.28–1.01). Trial mortality was 26% against 10% in contemporaneous non-trial patients at the same centres, so neither arm's figure is the expected risk of either route. And ESGE's own section prints a meta-analysis giving percutaneous drainage higher therapeutic success (OR 3.5, 2.1–6.0) and 11.5-fold more reintervention after ERCP, 10 of its 11 studies retrospective — its strong recommendation runs against the best comparative data beside it. The 7.8%-versus-17.1% seeding differential that drives the ASGE recommendation is, by that panel's own assessment, the weakest evidence in its document: a six-study meta-analysis with high heterogeneity (I² 66%) and very few events, plus one adjusted single-centre cohort giving percutaneous drainage as the only independent predictor of peritoneal recurrence (OR 6.9, 1.9–25.7), both graded very low quality behind a conditional recommendation. Treat it as a reason to prefer the endoscopic route where a curative option survives, not as a measured seeding rate.

honest.t: The drainage volume targets — more than 50%, ideally 70% or more, and better still above 80% — have never been derived, and this page now grades them D.
honest.why: No meta-analysis or comparative trial has tested any percentage threshold. The supporting cohorts disagree among themselves (50%, 71%, 80%), the 50% and 80% figures come from single-centre retrospective series, both guideline statements are graded low or very low quality, and ESGE lists prospective volumetry against survival and access to chemotherapy as an unmet need. The sector arithmetic (30/30/30/10) is a planning convention, not a measurement.

honest.t: Two stent choices are unsettled and the page takes a position on neither: bilateral versus unilateral, and metal versus plastic.
honest.why: ASGE suggests bilateral stenting absent lobar atrophy, but its pooled survival gain was 11 days (95% CI −12 to 35), pooled patency showed no difference (SMD 0.38, −0.22 to 0.99, I² 78%), technical success was lower, and the panel worried a strong recommendation would burden endoscopists without the expertise. ESGE 2026 cites one randomised trial favouring bilateral stenting on clinical success (95.3% versus 84.9%) and patency (252 versus 139 days). Both panels carry declared relationships with stent manufacturers. This needs a local default rather than per-case improvisation. The metal-versus-plastic comparison is separately confounded: the pooled advantage for metal stents — 56 days more survival (12–101), better patency, fewer reinterventions (OR 0.34) — comes from trials that waited for plastic stents to occlude rather than exchanging them on schedule, which is why the ASGE panel declined a strong recommendation. If this programme exchanges plastic stents on schedule, the comparator arm in those trials is not the practice being compared against.

honest.t: The transplant protocol's intention-to-treat result and its per-protocol result are different numbers on different denominators, and the draft blurred them.
honest.why: Intention-to-treat survival from the start of therapy was 68% at 2 years and 53% at 5 years in all 287 patients. Recurrence-free survival of 78% and 65% is measured among the 214 who reached transplantation, after 71 of 287 (25%) had dropped out at a median of 4.6 months. Excluding the 15 patients (5%) transplanted on clinical suspicion with no histologic proof, 5-year intention-to-treat survival was 50% and recurrence-free survival 62%. A patient entering this pathway should be quoted the first set, not the second. Two further figures from the same series are routinely misread. The hazard ratio of 2.98 (95% CI 1.79–4.95) for patients transplanted off criteria is for a composite group — 21 patients with a mass over 3 cm, 16 with a direct tumour biopsy, 4 with metastases and 7 with a prior malignancy, analysed together, with mass size producing the largest single disparity (5-year recurrence-free survival 32% versus 69%) — so it is not attributable to any one violation and in particular not to biopsy alone. And the widely quoted 5-year figures of 55–65% in primary sclerosing cholangitis and 35–55% in de novo disease are an ungraded 2015 expert consensus written by six people from four institutions, not a result of this series, which found no difference in outcome by PSC status at all; the page no longer quotes them as protocol outcomes.

honest.t: The seeding evidence behind the biopsy prohibition is six exposed patients and five events, and reverse causation is not excluded.
honest.why: Of 191 protocol patients, 16 had an outside transperitoneal aspirate; 5 of the 6 whose aspirate was positive had peritoneal metastases at staging against 8% (14 of 175) of those not biopsied, while all 9 with non-diagnostic aspirates were metastasis-free. Because only diagnostic aspirates carried the excess, a positive aspirate may be marking a tumour bulky and cell-rich enough to hit with a needle. The groups could not be matched on tumour differentiation or perineural invasion because the diagnostic tissue was too limited, and only patients already accepted onto the protocol were counted, so anyone whose outside aspirate removed them from consideration is invisible. The prohibition stands as a policy condition; it is not a measured risk.

honest.t: Two of the protocol's alternative diagnostic criteria — FISH polysomy and CA 19-9 above 100 U/mL — are weaker than their place in a listing decision implies.
honest.why: Pooled polysomy sensitivity is 51% (43–59) at 93% specificity (91–95), but roughly three in ten benign PSC strictures test positive on any FISH result, and polysomy alone can qualify a patient for neoadjuvant chemoradiation and transplantation. All eight studies in that meta-analysis came from one centre with overlapping recruitment windows, so the pooled estimate is effectively one institution's experience, and verification bias is likely because a FISH-positive patient is more likely to reach the surgery that classifies them. Trisomy or tetrasomy alone is uninformative and must not be counted (positive likelihood ratio 1.19, 0.65–2.21). CA 19-9 is the other: pooled accuracy for separating benign from malignant stricture is 81% (76–87) with a 15% false-positive rate, from a recommendation graded very low quality, and the marker rises in primary sclerosing cholangitis, cirrhosis and obstructive jaundice — all three of which describe this population. Record the bilirubin and drainage status with every value, and do not let an undrained or cholangitic measurement count toward candidacy.

honest.t: The sampling numbers on this page were cited from the smaller and more favourable pooled estimate, and how much tissue to take is itself unsettled.
honest.why: ESGE's 25% (11–38, OR 2.7) comes from two retrospective cohorts totalling 101 patients. ASGE's 20% (9–31) comes from 21 studies and 2,726 patients, with combined sensitivity 0.66 against 0.52 for biopsy and 0.40 for brushing. The page now leads with the larger estimate. Both recommendations are conditional on very low quality evidence and neither panel found a randomised trial for any perihilar question. The quantity question is live and the two sources disagree in a way that matters: ESGE says three to four intraductal biopsies appear sufficient, while the real-world cholangioscopy cohort took a median of three and had 33% of specimens inconclusive, and its authors recommend a minimum of four with a pathologist on site, noting that series reporting under 6% inconclusive took at least four. Cytology sensitivity rises monotonically with brush passes — 38% at 10, 47% at 20, 57% at 30. A local minimum for passes and biopsies would convert this from technique to policy.

honest.t: Cholangioscopy is presented in the guidelines as having no excess adverse events. In practice it has them.
honest.why: The pooled guideline statement found no difference in adverse events, specimen adequacy or technical success. The PSC meta-analysis records post-procedure cholangitis in 11% and procedural failure in 15% of PSC ducts against 2% of controls, because the cholangioscope often cannot pass a tight stricture without dilation and mucosal trauma. The real-world cohort had adverse events in 10 of 80 (13%): two episodes of bacterial cholangitis, one post-ERCP pancreatitis, and one cardiac arrest during the procedure followed by stroke. The pooled cholangioscopy advantage also rests on 4 studies and 128 patients, with study quality itself contributing significantly to the heterogeneity, and the senior authors declaring consultancy for the manufacturers of the platforms that came out best.

honest.t: The sequencing panel's headline figures come from a study in which sequencing and pathology were never run on the same specimen, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay.
honest.why: Specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, 5% of patients had no follow-up and were dropped, FISH — the adjunct many units actually use in PSC — was never compared head to head, and a stricture could be classified as neoplastic on imaging plus 12 months of clinical or radiographic progression rather than on tissue, which tends to flatter the test that often prompted the work-up. Only 2% of neoplastic strictures were purely dysplastic, so outside PSC this is earlier diagnosis of established cancer rather than early detection, and no survival or resectability benefit has been shown. The test is a laboratory-developed test from a single CLIA-certified laboratory, not FDA cleared. And in the one real-world cohort that reported this disease separately, the gain in cholangiocarcinoma itself was not significant: 75% versus 42.9% overall in 77 patients, but 70% versus 60% (P=.72) in the 20 with cholangiocarcinoma, with the headline improvement driven partly by pancreatic and ampullary cancers; in that cohort's PSC subgroup sensitivity was 20% against 40% for brush cytology, and the panel was run only on brush and bile aspirate, never on transpapillary or cholangioscopy-guided tissue. A negative sequencing result does not stand a resection decision down — negative predictive value was 63% in the developer's prospective series (37 false negatives, 25%) and 74–82% in a small real-world cohort whose benign cases rested on six months of follow-up.

honest.t: The resection recommendation's margin data come from 23 resections over 30 years, in a series where only 9 of 122 operated patients achieved a histologically negative margin.
honest.why: Downgraded from B to C. There was no comparison group — patients treated by bypass or intubation were never analysed — follow-up averaged 26 months, and the 3-year figures rest on very few patients at risk. The R0 ranges the page quotes alongside (median survival 27–58 months, 5-year 27–45%) are ungraded expert consensus. What survives this reading is the direction, which is unambiguous and consistent across every later series: margin status drives outcome, and local excision alone above type I does not achieve it.

honest.t: The Milan consensus prefers left-sided to right-sided hemihepatectomy where both would clear the tumour, and the page previously said nothing about laterality.
honest.why: Right-sided resection carries more morbidity, post-hepatectomy liver failure and mortality at equal oncological outcome in the jury's reading, and left trisectionectomy is favoured in Bismuth-Corlette type 4. That recommendation sits at level-4 expert opinion in a document where 84% of 570 reviewed studies were observational and 83.5% only of acceptable quality. It belongs in the operative conversation as a preference to be argued, not a rule.

honest.t: Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma has no validated resectability tool, and the body that said so most clearly is the one whose criteria the page relies on.
honest.why: The Milan jury declined to endorse any staging system — Bismuth-Corlette and MSKCC included — as a predictor of resectability, and states that the resectability criteria it adopted are expert-opinion-based and require validation. Only 32 of its 570 reviewed studies (5.6%) concerned transplantation. Resectability at this board is therefore a judgement by experienced surgeons looking at the same images, and should be recorded as such.

honest.t: The adjuvant evidence in this disease is a trial that missed its primary endpoint and a trial that was null, and both need reading in full.
honest.why: BILCAP missed its intention-to-treat primary endpoint (HR 0.81, 0.63–1.04, p=0.097); significance came from a per-protocol analysis and a model adjusted for nodal status, grade and sex. Recurrence-free survival favoured capecitabine over the first 24 months (HR 0.75, 0.58–0.98) and not at all from 24 to 60 months (HR 1.48, 0.80–2.77). 128 of 447 patients (29%) had hilar tumours, the trial was not powered for site, and the Milan consensus records no benefit in the perihilar subgroup. Grade 3 events in 44%, 46% dose-reduced, 32% stopped for toxicity. Offer it with those numbers, not as an obligation. The one adjuvant randomised trial confined to this population, BCAT, enrolled perihilar and distal bile duct cancer only and found nothing for gemcitabine (overall survival HR 1.01, 0.70–1.45), with no subgroup benefiting including node-positive and R1 patients — but its null is also underpowered: recruitment stopped at 226 of a planned 300 because most patients wanted adjuvant chemotherapy, the authors calculate only a 2.8% probability of significance even with the planned events, and observed 5-year survival was about 50% against an assumed 30% in a cohort from which R2 resections, metastases, severe complications and in-hospital deaths were all excluded. It rules out gemcitabine; it does not rule out adjuvant therapy.

honest.t: First-line chemo-immunotherapy is graded B rather than A on this page, because the subgroup that contains perihilar disease showed no effect.
honest.why: Both trials are properly conducted positive phase 3 trials in biliary tract cancer as a whole, but KEYNOTE-966 was enriched for intrahepatic disease (59%, because tumour tissue was mandatory) and its extrahepatic subgroup hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% CI 0.73–1.35), with the gallbladder subgroup at 0.96 (0.73–1.26); the authors state both are underpowered. KEYNOTE-966 also missed its progression-free survival boundary and showed identical response rates (29% versus 29%). TOPAZ-1 was a prespecified interim analysis at 424 of 496 planned deaths, powered to about 75%, with a formally violated proportional hazards assumption and a 1.3-month median gain concentrated after 6 months. The regimen remains the standard; the effect size in this disease is an extrapolation and should be described as one.

honest.t: The matched-therapy trials are not trials in this disease, with one instructive exception.
honest.why: FIGHT-202 cohort A was 107 of 108 intrahepatic, FOENIX-CCA2 intrahepatic only, ROAR 39 of 43 (91%) intrahepatic, ClarIDHy 6 of 187 extrahepatic or perihilar. All are single-arm or, in ClarIDHy's case, randomised against placebo with a non-significant intention-to-treat overall survival (HR 0.79, 0.56–1.12) and a 2% response rate. All were industry sponsored with company employees as authors, and all sit second line or later. HER2 is the exception, because it is enriched in extrahepatic disease: zanidatamab gave a 52% response rate in immunohistochemistry 3+ tumours against 6% (1 of 18) in 2+, with median overall survival 18.1 versus 5.2 months — so the assay threshold carries the result, and ESMO concedes there are no standardised criteria for assessing HER2 in this disease and no specific test it can recommend.

honest.t: The liver-directed avoid rows are graded D, not C: they rest on the absence of perihilar evidence rather than on comparative studies.
honest.why: No study in this depot addresses ablation, radioembolisation, chemoembolisation or histotripsy of a central perihilar primary. The hepatic arterial infusion data are from a single-arm, single-institution trial in liver-confined intrahepatic disease that treated 38 of 84 screened patients, with grade 4 pump or arterial complications in 11% and biliary stents needed in 11%, two for chemotherapy-induced biliary sclerosis — the one toxicity that matters most in a tumour whose problem is central biliary obstruction. The roadmap's positions stand; what changes is that they are honest absences of evidence rather than graded comparisons.

honest.t: The best-supportive-care bundle was graded A. It is not one intervention and only part of it has evidence in this depot.
honest.why: Downgraded to C. Drainage rests on guideline recommendations graded low to very low quality; early specialist palliative involvement rests on randomised evidence in other cancers that this reference depot does not contain; pruritus control, pain control and nutritional support are uncontroversial but untested here. The bundle is right; the grade was reading as though a trial had tested it.

honest.t: Device-industry relationships run through most of the evidence this page depends on for drainage, stenting and cholangioscopy.
honest.why: Five ESGE 2026 authors declare consultancy, advisory or lecture relationships with stent manufacturers; many ASGE panel members declare the same across both the hilar-obstruction and the stricture-diagnosis guidelines; multiple ESGE 2025 panel members declare relationships with endoscopy device manufacturers; and the senior authors of the PSC meta-analysis that puts cholangioscopy first declare consultancy for the manufacturers of the cholangioscopy platforms. None of these guidelines was industry funded. This is not a reason to discount them, but it is a reason to read a strong recommendation on moderate evidence carefully, and it should be on the table when the programme ratifies a route or a stent default. One ASGE panel member on the hilar-obstruction guideline is at this institution.

board: Submission — an Epic form captures the clinical question, biliary anatomy and drainage status, bilirubin trajectory, resectability assessment, remnant volume, transplant-protocol candidacy, prior treatment, referring clinician and urgency. Owner: submitting clinician.

Triage — a coordinator and a clinically trained gatekeeper check completeness, imaging quality, duplicate cases, the urgent lane, and whether the question is actually a decision question. Owners: coordinator and chair.
Agenda — stable at least 24 hours ahead, approximately 10–12 decision cases per session, each case carrying one focused question. Owner: coordinator.
Urgent lane — a same-week slot with chair approval. In this disease the urgent lane is used routinely: cholangitis and a rising bilirubin are time-critical. Owner: chair.

Attendance — hepatobiliary and transplant surgery, medical oncology, radiation oncology, interventional radiology, advanced endoscopy, diagnostic radiology, pathology, hepatology and coordination are all required. Owners: specialty leads.

Imaging — adequate and current imaging reviewed before the recommendation, with MRI/MRCP obtained before stenting wherever possible because stents degrade assessment of ductal extent. Owner: diagnostic radiology.
Pathology — pre-alerted for every case requiring confirmation, and for every case where transplant-protocol candidacy depends on establishing malignancy. Owner: pathology.
Output — one recommendation, one owner, one due date, one reassessment date, one documented alternative considered; drain ownership is named separately. Owner: chair.
Documentation — an Epic note within one business day, in the agreed structured format. Owner: named owner.
Registry — the case closed in the registry with the decision, the modality delivered, drainage events and the outcome at reassessment. Owner: coordinator.

Referring relationships — the referring clinician is informed of the recommendation and of who owns the next step. Community-referring relationships are protected explicitly: the pathway returns patients with a plan, it does not capture them. Owner: named owner.
dashboard: Drainage route, cholangitis episodes and re-intervention rate, by route (§11 item 2).
Drains per patient and cholangitis episodes, against a named drain owner (§11 item 7).
Post-hepatectomy liver failure by preoperative bilirubin, to test the local bilirubin threshold (§11 item 3).
Annual volume of extended hepatectomy with biliary reconstruction, 90-day mortality and R0 rate (§11 item 4).
Biopsy route in every potentially protocol-eligible patient (§11 item 6).
Next-generation sequencing result, the protocol decision taken on it, and the explant finding (§11 item 8).
Adjuvant capecitabine uptake, completion and recurrence (§11 item 5).
Margin status, nodal status, adjuvant modality, and local and distant recurrence (§11 item 10).
Registry closure: decision, modality delivered, drainage events and outcome at reassessment, for every case (§10).

Reassessment adherence: within 1–2 weeks after drainage, 3–6 weeks after portal vein embolisation, every 8–12 weeks on systemic therapy, every 3–6 months for 2 years after resection, and per protocol on the transplant pathway (§9).

approvals.q: Does the programme open a perihilar transplant protocol, and under whose governance?
approvals.why: Supporting data are retrospective multicentre protocol experience with heavy selection. Graft stewardship is an institutional judgement.

approvals.q: Endoscopic or percutaneous drainage as the default first route?
approvals.why: The randomised trial was negative on its primary endpoint (severe drainage-related complications 63% versus 67%, RR 0.94), enrolled 54 of a planned 106 patients and stopped early because mortality was higher after percutaneous drainage (41% versus 11%; cause unexplained, authors call the signal prone to type I error). Pooled across three trials 30-day mortality only trended lower with the endoscopic route (RR 0.53, 0.28–1.01). ESGE's own section gives percutaneous drainage higher therapeutic success (OR 3.5) and 11.5-fold less reintervention. Local endoscopic and interventional radiology expertise decides.

approvals.q: Bilirubin threshold before major hepatectomy, embolic therapy, radiation, and systemic therapy.
approvals.why: No comparative data define the cut-off; it is a safety convention.
approvals.audit: Audit: post-hepatectomy liver failure by preoperative bilirubin.

approvals.q: Minimum annual volume for extended hepatectomy with biliary reconstruction at this centre.
approvals.why: Volume-outcome relationships are observational but consistent. The threshold is a governance choice. [EXPERTISE]

approvals.q: Adjuvant capecitabine — offered routinely, or case-by-case?
approvals.why: BILCAP's primary analysis was not significant and BCAT was null for gemcitabine in bile duct cancer specifically.

approvals.q: How is tissue obtained in a potentially protocol-eligible patient?
approvals.why: A protocol condition, not an evidence question, but it requires a standing agreement so no one disqualifies a candidate inadvertently.
approvals.audit: Audit: biopsy route in protocol candidates.

approvals.q: Who owns drain management across services?
approvals.why: Not an evidence question. Uncoordinated drainage is a recognised failure pattern and needs a named owner.
approvals.audit: Audit: drains per patient, cholangitis episodes.

approvals.q: Does a molecular (next-generation sequencing) result on an ERCP-obtained specimen satisfy the transplant protocol's confirmed-malignancy condition?
approvals.why: The published protocol criteria predate these data and do not address molecular confirmation. Diagnostic performance is now supported by a prospective multi-institutional study, but the protocol question is a governance decision, not an evidence one. [PAYER]
approvals.audit: Decide in advance with the transplant team; registry: NGS result, protocol decision, explant finding. The developing centre reports already using these results to inform transplant decision-making in selected patients — precedent worth asking about directly, though their protocol is not ours.

approvals.q: Who owns subsequent NCCN and OPTN update checks, and on what cycle?
approvals.why: Source reconciliation is complete in this version. Assign an owner to verify subsequent editions and current allocation requirements, ratify the documented institutional positions, and maintain the update cycle.
approvals.audit: Named owner plus edition and date, with an agreed update cycle.

approvals.q: Adjuvant chemoradiation after R0 resection with nodal metastases?
approvals.why: NCCN places nodal involvement alongside margin status as a trigger for discussing chemoradiation; BSG 2023 limits its recommendation to R1 resection, and the node-positive benefit rests on retrospective meta-analysis.
approvals.audit: Registry: margin status, nodal status, adjuvant modality, local and distant recurrence.

approvals.q: Which palliative drainage volume target does the programme adopt — NCCN's more than 50%, or ESGE 2026's ideally 70% or more?
approvals.why: Neither was derived. No comparative trial or meta-analysis has tested a percentage threshold, the supporting cohorts disagree (50%, 71%, 80%), and both guideline statements are graded low or very low quality. The choice is a planning convention and should be written down rather than left to the endoscopist at the index ERCP.
approvals.audit: Registry: percentage of viable non-atrophic volume drained, cholangitis, re-intervention, time to first systemic therapy cycle.

approvals.q: Is first-line chemo-immunotherapy offered on the biliary-tract-wide result, given that the extrahepatic subgroup showed no effect?
approvals.why: KEYNOTE-966's extrahepatic subgroup hazard ratio was 0.99 (0.73–1.35) and the trial was enriched for intrahepatic disease; TOPAZ-1 was an interim analysis with a violated proportional hazards assumption and a 1.3-month median gain. The roadmap's position is to offer it; the group should agree how it is described to a perihilar patient, because the honest answer is an extrapolation.
approvals.audit: Registry: regimen, immune-mediated events, 12- and 24-month survival by anatomical subsite.

approvals.q: Bilateral or unilateral stenting as the default in palliative hilar obstruction?
approvals.why: ASGE suggests bilateral absent lobar atrophy on a pooled survival gain of 11 days (95% CI −12 to 35) and no pooled patency difference; one randomised trial reported in ESGE 2026 favours bilateral on patency. Both panels carry declared stent-manufacturer relationships. Without a default this is decided case by case by whoever is holding the scope.
approvals.audit: Registry: number of stents, sectors drained, patency, re-intervention.

approvals.q: Does FISH polysomy alone satisfy the programme's diagnostic threshold for entering a patient on the transplant protocol?
approvals.why: Polysomy is a named protocol criterion, but its positive predictive value in primary sclerosing cholangitis is 0.68, roughly three in ten benign PSC strictures are positive on any FISH result, and all eight studies in the pooled estimate came from one centre with overlapping cohorts. Trisomy and tetrasomy alone must be excluded explicitly, since their positive likelihood ratio is 1.19. A written local rule prevents a benign stricture entering neoadjuvant chemoradiation.
approvals.audit: Registry: diagnostic criterion used at protocol entry, and the explant finding.

approvals.q: A written minimum for brush passes and intraductal biopsies at the index ERCP.
approvals.why: ESGE says three to four biopsies appear sufficient; the real-world cohort that took a median of three had 33% inconclusive specimens and 15% biopsy sensitivity, and its authors recommend at least four. Cytology sensitivity rises with passes — 38% at 10, 47% at 20, 57% at 30. This is the cheapest available improvement in yield on the one sampling route that does not jeopardise protocol candidacy.
approvals.audit: Audit: brush passes and biopsy number per index ERCP, inconclusive-specimen rate, sensitivity against final diagnosis.

approvals.q: Left-sided versus right-sided hepatectomy where both would achieve R0.
approvals.why: The Milan consensus prefers left-sided hemihepatectomy on the grounds of lower morbidity, liver failure and mortality at equal oncological outcome, and favours left trisectionectomy in Bismuth-Corlette type 4. That sits at level-4 expert opinion, so it is a preference for the group to accept or decline rather than a rule to import.
approvals.audit: Registry: laterality, remnant volume, post-hepatectomy liver failure, 90-day mortality, R0 rate.

provenance: Revised on 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of this page's reference depot. All 39 PubMed-indexed references were read in full and abstracted with an independent critique: 19 from the perihilar cholangiocarcinoma depot and 20 shared papers drawn from the intrahepatic CCA depot, which supplies the biliary systemic-therapy trials (ABC-02, TOPAZ-1, KEYNOTE-966, ABC-06, BILCAP, BCAT, PRODIGE-12, ASCOT), the targeted-therapy trials (ClarIDHy, FIGHT-202, FOENIX-CCA2, ROAR, HERIZON-BTC-01), the hepatic arterial infusion trial, the AASLD, BSG, ESMO 2023 and ESMO 2024 interim guidelines, and the two next-generation sequencing studies from the developing centre. Three limits of that read should be named rather than implied. First, one reference is effectively abstract-level: in Gillmeister 2026 (PMID 42698384, a brief report) the Results section did not survive text extraction, so every figure quoted from it comes from its Table 1, abstract and Discussion and is expressed per biopsy rather than per patient, and its patient count, malignancy prevalence and PSC subgroup size could not be read. Second, several linked editorials and correspondence were identified in PubMed but not obtained in full, so no critique point on this page is attributed to them: Alipour's editorial on Bardhi 2025 (PMID 40518235), Bridgewater, Webster and Amin's comment on the DRAINAGE trial (PMID 30122357), the four ABC-06 correspondence letters, and the paywalled Lancet Oncology comments on ClarIDHy, where the cost-of-benefit point is reported second-hand and should be treated as provisional. Third, SWOG S0809 is cited only as quoted by BSG 2023; the primary report is not in this depot, and the non-PubMed sources — NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9, the OPTN review-board guidance, the UTHealth protocol v2, the HOPE4LIVER one-year update, the roadmap itself and its alignment worksheet — were read as documents but not abstracted or critiqued in the same way. Where a figure in the earlier draft could not be traced to any of these sources it has been replaced with one that can, and the removals are visible in the text: the reported incidence split for IDH1 between intrahepatic and extrahepatic disease, and a per-site adjuvant hazard ratio for hilar tumours, are both gone. Built from the Memorial Hermann Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6, dated 4 October 2026 (with the liver-directed treatment revision of 3 October 2026), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same version and date, which compares AASLD 2023, BSG 2023, the ESMO 2024 interim update, the Asia-Pacific 2024 consensus, OPTN policy and review-board guidance, and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 (10 March 2026) across sixteen areas.
